lesson.title: Zip: Weaving Two Lists Into Pairs
lesson.summary: The zip() function walks multiple iterables side by side, bundling their matching elements into tuples so you can process related data together.
lesson.body:
It is common to have two related Lists that are meant to line up position by position: a list of student names and a parallel list of their scores, or a list of product names and a list of their prices. Looping over one list with an index and then reaching into the other list at that same index works, but it is easy to get the indexing wrong and the code reads awkwardly. The built-in zip() function solves this directly: it walks several iterables at once and, for each step, bundles the current element from each one into a Tuple.

names = ["Ana", "Ben", "Cleo"]
scores = [92, 85, 78]

pairs = list(zip(names, scores))
print(pairs)

for name, score in zip(names, scores):
    print(name, "scored", score)

The first print shows [('Ana', 92), ('Ben', 85), ('Cleo', 78)]: zip paired each name with the score that shares its position, and wrapping the result in list() forces Python to build all the tuples at once so you can see them. The loop below it prints three lines, Ana scored 92, then Ben scored 85, then Cleo scored 78, because each pass through the loop unpacks one of those tuples straight into the names name and score.

zip() does not require its inputs to be the same length, but it will not complain if they are not: it simply stops as soon as the shortest iterable runs out.

ids = [1, 2, 3, 4]
letters = ["a", "b"]
print(list(zip(ids, letters)))

This prints [(1, 'a'), (2, 'b')]. The values 3 and 4 in ids are simply never paired with anything, because letters ran out after two items. That silent stopping is worth remembering: if a bug in your code involves missing data at the end of a zipped loop, mismatched list lengths are a good first suspect.
